More than twenty states have now sued the same nine companies over insulin prices. Florida filed this week. Texas, California, Utah, Minnesota, Michigan, Iowa, Missouri, Oregon, Delaware, Indiana, Massachusetts, Kansas, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kentucky, Illinois and Arizona got there first.

Red states, blue states, and every single complaint describes the same scheme with the same defendants.

The defendants are always three manufacturers who make over 90% of the world's insulin, three PBMs who process roughly 80% of American prescriptions, and the rebate aggregators that sit between them. Florida named those too. Zinc, Ascent and Emisar, the offshore entities the rebate money gets routed through.

The mechanism, per Florida's complaint: manufacturers inflate the published list price, pay a cut back to the PBM, and get rewarded with preferred formulary placement. Both sides make more money every time the sticker price goes up. A Lilly executive testified that on a $280 vial of Humalog, roughly $210 goes back to the PBMs. That's 75% of the price of insulin functioning as a payment for permission to be covered.

Insulin costs around two dollars to manufacture.

If you want to know how locked in this is, look at what happened when somebody tried to break it. Novo Nordisk cut the list price of its insulin Levemir by 65%. Coverage for the drug collapsed from about 90% down to 35%. The PBMs dropped it because a cheaper drug pays them less. Novo discontinued it entirely.

Their CEO told a Senate committee in September 2024 that this is exactly why he won't cut list prices on his other drugs. His position was that a high list price is more likely to get patients access, because the middlemen only cover what pays them well. He also testified that 74 cents of every dollar the company brings in goes back to PBMs and insurers.

Sanders showed up to that hearing with written commitments from all three major PBMs promising they wouldn't drop coverage if Novo lowered prices. The CEO still wouldn't do it. He'd already learned what happens.

And the people who get charged against the inflated number are the ones with the least protection. Uninsured patients. People sitting in a deductible. Anyone on percentage coinsurance. The fake price was built to fund the rebate, and the patients with the worst coverage are the ones who pay it.

We don't take rebates. Nobody pays us for placement, and there's no list price to inflate because there's no middleman here to inflate it for. You pay what the drug costs plus a flat fee.

Your insurance company can count the machinery it uses to deny your care as money spent on your care.

Here's the rule that's supposed to prevent that. Under the ACA, insurers have to spend 80 to 85 cents of every premium dollar on actual medical care. It's called the medical loss ratio. They keep the rest for overhead and profit.

Medicare Advantage plans reported a medical loss ratio of almost 90% for 2023. Then the Insurance Watchdog Coalition went into those same plans' CMS filings and pulled out only the real medical and prescription claims. 82.5%. Below the legal minimum, and about $36 billion less than what got reported.

So what filled the gap? Per the report, the rules let plans count things that aren't medical care as if they were. Parts of prior authorization systems get classified as "quality improvement." Gym memberships count. Cash cards for everyday expenses count.

The apparatus that makes your doctor stop, fill out forms, and wait for permission to treat you gets filed in the same column as your treatment.

And that 82.5% still leaves something out. It doesn't break out what insurers pay the doctors, pharmacies and PBMs they own. UnitedHealth employs or is affiliated with around 90,000 physicians. CVS owns Aetna, Caremark, and its own clinics.

We don't have a medical loss ratio, because we don't have premiums. You pay for the medication plus a flat fee. There's nothing to reclassify.

A hospital wanted $18,000 to remove a polyp. The same procedure in a doctor's office runs about $3,000.

Her own professional society, ACOG, says it can be done right in an office with local numbing. So she found an OB who agreed to do it that way. Took the two-week course of hormones to prep for it.

Day before the procedure, his office calls. He can't do it in the office anymore. Has to be at a freestanding surgery center owned by the same health system, because that system bought his practice in 2025. She walks in the next morning to surgical techs and OR nurses moving around a room she didn't need. Bill came to about $6,000.

Want to know what the procedure actually involved? She turned down the sedation entirely. Doctor numbed her cervix, removed the polyp in a few minutes. She called it a few seconds of cramping. She spent it watching the images and talking to the OR crew about snorkeling.

A few minutes of work, and three different prices depending on which room they put her in.

82% of physicians in this country now work for a hospital, an insurer, another corporate entity, or private equity. UnitedHealth alone employs around 10,000 primary care doctors and has another 80,000 affiliated. When somebody owns your doctor, they also own the decision about where your procedure happens.

Almost none of it gets reviewed. Mergers only trigger antitrust reporting above a dollar threshold, currently around $134 million. Yale researchers looked at more than 275 hospital acquisitions of physician practices and found over 99% fell below that line. It happens one small practice at a time until there's no independent left in your county.

And the results are measured. When Harvard researchers studied hospitals buying gastroenterology groups, prices went up, quality went down, complication rates rose. The one thing that got better was throughput. That's a financial number, not a medical one.

Same machine runs at the pharmacy counter. Your insurer owns the PBM, the PBM owns the specialty pharmacy, and you get routed to whichever one pays them most, whether or not it's cheapest or even has your drug in stock.

We're not attached to any of it. No insurer, no PBM, no parent company deciding where you're allowed to go. Cost plus a flat fee, posted before you pay.

A tweet went around this week saying it's hard to research healthcare without concluding that insurance companies are heroes. 2.5 million views. His argument was that somebody has to tell doctors no, and the insurance company is the one brave enough to do it.

The problem with that argument is that the insurance company is the doctor now.

UnitedHealth's Optum arm employs or is affiliated with more than 90,000 physicians. That's roughly one in ten doctors in this country working for a company that also owns an insurer and a PBM. CVS owns Aetna and Oak Street Health. Cigna, Humana, Elevance all have provider arms. The referee bought the team.

So who exactly is telling whom no?

A Health Affairs study published last November found UnitedHealthcare pays its own Optum-affiliated doctors about 17 percent more than it pays outside doctors for the same work. Not less. More. They're not holding the line on costs, they're routing money from one pocket to another and calling the higher number a negotiated rate.

Under the ACA, insurers have to spend 80 to 85 cents of every premium dollar on actual care. Their margin is capped as a percentage. Think about what that does to the incentive. If you can only keep 15 percent, the only way to make more money next year is for the whole pie to get bigger. Higher prices. More utilization. Bigger premiums.

They don't profit by saying no. They profit when the total goes up.

That's why costs never come down no matter how many "cost containment" programs get announced. A company whose profit is a fixed slice of total spending has no reason to shrink total spending. Shrinking it is the one thing that actually hurts them.

The guy who wrote that thread was looking at prior authorizations and denials and seeing discipline. What's actually happening is a company denying your claim on Monday and paying its own clinic a premium rate on Tuesday, with your premium funding both.

There's a version of this with nobody in the middle. We don't bill insurance. There's no PBM setting our price, no parent company we route money to, no incentive for our number to go up. We buy the drug, add a flat fee, and post it.

A guy looked at his urgent care bill and caught them.

Clinic said the visit was $1,200. Insurance took credit for negotiating it down. He checked his benefits. Insurance paid nothing. Zero. He paid $620 out of his own pocket.

So the $1,200 was made up. The savings were made up. The only real number in that whole transaction was $620, and it came out of his wallet after he'd already been paying premiums all year.

Nobody pays $1,200 for urgent care. A simple visit, a cough, a UTI, a refill, posts at $100 to $250 cash at most clinics. The $1,200 exists so the discount has something to point at. That's the only reason that number is on the page.

He could have walked into that same clinic, said nothing about insurance, and asked for the self-pay price. Most urgent cares will knock another 15 to 40 percent off for paying that day. He'd have been out maybe $150.

Instead he paid $620 for the privilege of watching a fake discount get applied to a fake price.

Call around before you go. Two or three places, ask what the visit costs cash, ten minutes on the phone. You'll know more about the price than anyone standing at that front desk will tell you.

Better option, look at direct primary care. Flat monthly fee, no insurance in the middle, a doctor who knows you and picks up the phone. That's what we do for our family.

The same trick runs at the pharmacy counter. Inflated price, invented discount, a copay with no relationship to what the drug actually costs.

We fired the people who inflate the number. Cost plus a flat fee, posted before you pay.

A guy went viral this week telling people to use GoodRx to escape their insurance pricing. He is right that your insurance price is probably too high. He is wrong about what GoodRx is.

GoodRx does not negotiate anything. It surfaces prices that pharmacy benefit managers already set. The same PBMs that built the price you are trying to escape. Express Scripts, OptumRx, CVS Caremark, MedImpact, Navitus. GoodRx has contracts with all of them.

Follow the money on a GoodRx fill. You hand over the coupon. The pharmacy processes that claim through a specific PBM. The pharmacy then pays a per-prescription fee to that PBM. The PBM shares a slice of that fee back to GoodRx for sending you there. GoodRx has reported earning roughly 15% of your total prescription cost.

So the PBM gets paid when you use your insurance, and the PBM gets paid when you use GoodRx to get around your insurance. Both roads lead to the same building.

The scale of this is not small. In 2020 alone GoodRx accounted for about $3.4 billion in prescription revenue and collected nearly $500 million in fees from PBMs. Three out of four people using GoodRx already had insurance. They were paying premiums every month and still needed a coupon to afford their own medication.

Sit with the shape of that. You pay a PBM premiums all year. That PBM sets a price so high you cannot use it. Then a company funded by that same PBM shows you a different price the PBM also set, and the PBM collects a fee on that transaction too.

Express Scripts made GoodRx its exclusive discount card provider for commercial members. CVS Caremark runs its own version. These are not competitors sneaking around the PBMs. These are the PBMs opening a second register.

Industry analysts have been blunt about why the two prices exist at all. Different PBMs have different contracted rates, legacy contracts do not reflect current market pricing, and the same PBM offers different rates to different clients. If the cash rate were easy to see, employers would demand it. The confusion is the product.

GoodRx is better than overpaying, and if it is what you have, use it. I would rather someone save $40 than not. But understand you are not escaping the system. You are using the system's back door and paying a toll to the same people who locked the front one.

A woman posted a bill for $34,000 for an MRI. Thirty-two thousand of that was hospital facility fees. She was not in a hospital.

She was at a place with a sign out front that says Imaging Center. She read the sign on camera. No hospital anywhere on it. But because that building is classified as a hospital outpatient department, the bill comes with hospital pricing attached. After insurance she still owes $1,336. She had an MRI in an actual ER a month earlier and paid a few hundred dollars.

Then comes the best part. She asked for a copy of her images on a CD. They told her they do not do that there, only hospitals do CDs. So the building is a hospital when it is time to bill her and not a hospital when she needs something from it.

Here is the mechanism nobody explains to patients. A hospital buys an imaging center or a physician practice, changes the billing designation to "hospital outpatient department," and the exact same scan on the exact same machine read by the exact same radiologist starts generating a facility fee that did not exist the week before. Nothing clinical changed. The paperwork changed.

The numbers on this are not subtle. Medicare pays roughly $475 for an MRI at an independent imaging center and roughly $720 for the identical scan at a hospital outpatient department. On the commercial side the gap is worse, independent centers commonly run $400 to $1,200 cash while hospital outpatient departments run $1,500 to $3,500 for the same images. Freestanding centers do not add a facility fee. Hospital outpatient departments do, on top of everything else, and the radiologist often bills separately too.

Same equipment. Same pictures. Same person reading them. Two to five times the price depending entirely on who owns the building.

This is also why independent doctors keep disappearing. If a hospital gets paid more than an independent practice for identical work, the independent practice cannot compete on those terms. It is not a fair fight, and it was never designed to be one. Competition is what drives quality up and prices down, and this arrangement removes the competition and calls it consolidation.

The deeper problem is what actually makes a healthcare business successful in this country. It is not being good at medicine. It is being good at billing insurance. That is where the money is. So when you see a wildly profitable healthcare organization, that is not evidence they deliver excellent care. It is evidence they are excellent at extracting money from claims.

That is why we fired the insurance companies. There is no facility fee here, no reclassification games, no version of our price that depends on who owns the building. You see the number before you pay it.

The FDA spent yesterday in a hearing about whether to approve psychedelics as prescription medication, and it is much closer than most people realize.

Compass Pathways has a synthetic treatment for depression. Definium has a formula for anxiety that just went three for three on phase 3 trials in twelve weeks. Compass is already submitting its application. The first FDA-approved psychedelic in American history is probably months away.

Most of the hearing was about who is supposed to be in the room with you while you are on it.

The current plan uses something called a dosing session monitor. That is a person whose job is to sit there and make sure you are okay. Not a therapist. Psychologists testified that the therapy is what makes these treatments work and stripping it out to cut costs is a mistake. Psychiatrists said patients need a full psychiatric workup first, partly because some conditions make a dose like this genuinely dangerous. Nurses said they are already licensed and could start Monday. And a clinic in rural Nevada pointed out that the FDA wants a physician reachable within fifteen minutes, which in rural Nevada is less of a regulation and more of a wish.

Then there is how this got moving in the first place. Joe Rogan stood behind Trump in the Oval Office for an executive order on medical psychedelics in April. Shortly after, three psychedelic companies received Commissioner's National Priority Review vouchers. A former White House drug policy advisor testified that drugs should get approved "through science and trials, not politics or podcasters," and argued the existing trials are small relative to the populations being targeted.

He is not the only one urging caution. A mother named Susan Sagy testified that her 21-year-old daughter Shira died following psychedelic use. She was not there to block approval. Her argument was that FDA approval carries enormous cultural weight, and the country should be ready for what happens after the label changes.

These are not complicated molecules. They are cheap to make. The day the FDA approves one, it stops being cheap. It becomes a branded product with a patent, a PBM contract, a formulary tier, and a prior authorization form. It will carry a price nobody could justify and a copay nobody can predict, and everyone will pay for it through their premiums whether they ever touch it or not.

That is the pattern with every drug that goes from obscure to approved. The chemistry does not change. The billing does.

A woman posted about a trip to Walgreens that is a perfect case study in how this whole system works.

She goes to buy blood glucose test strips. Walgreens brand, 100 count, sitting right on the shelf for $29 and change. She grabs it, brings it to the register, and it rings up at $75. She tells the cashier there must be a mistake. The cashier scans it again. Still $75. She holds up the box she pulled from the shelf, the one clearly marked $29. The cashier is just as confused as she is, takes the box, disappears for six minutes, and comes back with the answer: that exact box was supposed to be stocked behind the pharmacy counter, not on the open shelf. Same box, same product, same barcode. Behind the counter, $75. On the shelf where a customer can just grab it, $29.

Watch what that means. Nothing about the test strips changed. The only variable was which side of the counter the box was sitting on, because one side runs through insurance billing and the other does not.

I have seen this from the other side, because I own a pharmacy. Insurance contracts require us to set a higher list price specifically so the insurance company can apply a "discount" on top of it and claim they saved you money. The drug never cost that much. The insurance did not lower anything. It inflated the price first so the discount would have something to point at.

This is not a one-store glitch. Researchers looked at omeprazole, the generic heartburn medication you can buy over the counter for about 80 cents a pill. Medicare Part D paid $27.85 for that same pill. Across 19 common over-the-counter drugs in that study, Medicare paid more than the cash price on 16 of them, and researchers estimated the program could have saved $406 million by just paying the cash price instead. A separate federal audit released last month found Medicare Part D made $587.7 million in improper payments on drugs that had already switched to over-the-counter status and should never have been billed to insurance in the first place.

None of that is a rare mistake. It is what happens by default when the price gets set for the insurance claim instead of for the medicine.

We fired that model. Every price you see from us is the real one, insured or not, shelf or counter. Cost plus a flat fee, out in the open.

While Walgreens was closing 1,200 stores and CVS was quietly inheriting the customers, something else was happening at the same time that most people missed.

In July 2026, the FTC reached a settlement with CVS Caremark itself, over formulary design, rebating, and vertical integration the agency said artificially inflated the cost of insulin and other medications.  The FTC called it anticompetitive. The financial press called it smart strategy. Same facts, opposite verdicts, depending on which desk is writing about it.

It gets worse. Back in January, the House Judiciary Committee released its own investigation and found that CVS Caremark may have broken federal antitrust law by blocking independent pharmacies from using third-party "hub" services, tools that help smaller pharmacies cut costs and compete. According to the committee, CVS studied how those services worked, then rewrote its own network rules specifically to lock independents out of them. This was not aimed at Walgreens. It was aimed at pharmacies like mine.

So the pattern is not limited to one dying competitor. Caremark, Optum Rx, and Express Scripts together process about 80% of every prescription claim filed in this country. Three companies decide what nearly every pharmacy in America gets paid, and two of the three own massive retail and provider networks that answer to nobody but their own parent. Walgreens getting squeezed into 1,200 closures is not a one-off story about one struggling chain. It is what happens to anyone standing on the wrong side of that arrangement, whether it is a national chain or a single independent pharmacy trying to serve its own town.

Regulators on both sides of the aisle have now looked at this same company and reached the same conclusion twice in one year. The FTC calls it anticompetitive. Congress calls it a possible antitrust violation. Meanwhile, the arrangement that lets a company own the pharmacy and the entity that pays the pharmacy keeps running exactly as it did before either finding was published.

That is the part worth remembering next time someone describes vertical integration as a competitive advantage instead of what regulators on both sides just called it.

We are not on either side of that setup. No PBM, no rebate scheme, no rule written to lock anyone out. Just the real cost of your medication, plus a flat fee.

CVS Health is now facing at least five lawsuits from major hospital systems, all alleging the same thing: CVS quietly kept money that was supposed to go to hospitals treating low-income patients.

The program is 340B. It requires drug makers to sell certain medications at a discount to hospitals that serve a lot of low-income and uninsured patients. Mount Sinai, Michigan Medicine, the University of Kansas Health System, Henry Ford Health, and now Froedtert have all sued CVS Health, alleging the company's pharmacy benefit manager and pharmacy subsidiaries pocketed a share of those discounts instead of passing them through

Here is how the hospitals say it worked. A specialty drug claim gets processed at the standard rate first, because eligibility for the 340B discount often is not known yet. Weeks later, once the claim is flagged as 340B-eligible, CVS Caremark quietly reprices it lower and pays that reduced amount to the hospital, presenting it as the full reimbursement. The hospital never sees what the claim was actually paid at the higher rate. CVS keeps the difference. Froedtert's lawsuit puts a number on it: they say CVS kept about 62% of the savings that should have reached the hospital.

Across the five lawsuits, the hospitals say this cost them roughly a quarter of a billion dollars over five years. And Froedtert adds another detail: when the hospital asked to audit the payments, CVS refused, then terminated the pharmacy services agreement.

Think about who this program was built for. 340B exists so safety-net hospitals can stretch limited dollars further while caring for people who often cannot pay. The lawsuits allege that money got quietly rerouted into a PBM's profit margin instead. CVS owns the insurer, the PBM, and the pharmacy filling the prescription, so it is grading its own homework at every step of that transaction, and the hospitals say it graded in its own favor

None of this has gone to trial, and CVS has not admitted to any of it. But five separate health systems are now making the same allegation with the same mechanism, and that pattern is hard to write off as a coincidence.

This is what happens when one company sits on every side of the transaction. Nobody outside the building is watching, so the money finds its way to whoever built the system.

We do not have that problem, because we are not on every side of anything. No PBM, no insurer, no hidden repricing weeks after the fact. You see the actual cost of your medication before you pay it.

An investigation from City Journal this week looked at a California home health company whose Medicaid billing went from about $90,000 in 2018 to more than $17 million in 2023.

The company is California Home Health Agency, run by a man named Nathan Ogbatue. Over three years, reporters say it pulled in $34 to $36 million from Medicaid. In the same window, Ogbatue and his wife reportedly bought more than $7 million in California real estate, a $2.7 million Riverside mansion with a putting green and an archery range, a beach house, and other properties. Back in Nigeria, where he holds a traditional chief title, he built a palace, complete with golden statues of himself and his wife.

The reporters tried to confirm any of the business was real. The office is a Riverside strip mall unit with the blinds shut. The company has not filed a mandatory state utilization report since 2019, the kind of report that would verify the services it billed for. Fraud experts who reviewed the billing data said the volume of services billed is wildly outside the norm and carries, in their words, every red flag of a shell operation.

What gets me is the same thing every one of these stories has in common. A company can bill a government program tens of millions of dollars, skip a required report for six straight years, operate out of an office nobody seems to work in, and the money keeps arriving anyway. Whether or not this particular case ends in charges, the pattern only exists because the door is unguarded.

The reason is simple. Nobody spending that money is spending their own. When a real person pays a real bill with their own money, they check it. When the payer is a giant program with no one actually watching the account, the checks never happen, and the money flows to whoever games it best. City Journal has reported that experts estimate up to 40% of spending in California's largest home health program may be lost to fraud.

We built our pharmacy to be the opposite of an open vault. You see the real price of a medication, out in the open, and you pay it. No mystery billing, no shell in the middle, no bottomless account.

The government just showed CBS a warehouse full of Ferraris, a Bugatti, a Mercedes G-Wagon, game-worn Kobe Bryant sneakers, and a $1.5 million Mickey Mantle baseball card. All of it seized from one man who stole it from a Medicaid program.

His name is Paul Randall. This week a federal judge sentenced him to 30 years and ordered him to repay $178 million. In about 11 months, he ran roughly $269 million in fraudulent claims through California's Medi-Cal and got paid about $178 million of it. He bought seven properties, including an 8,500 square foot Orange County compound with a gate so far from the house you cannot see the front door from the street. He was living like a king off of us.

In early 2022, Medi-Cal temporarily suspended its requirement that providers get prior authorization before expensive drugs could be billed. They dropped the check while switching payment systems. Randall drove a truck through the gap. He paid kickbacks for patient information, paid a nurse practitioner to sign pre-filled prescriptions for 19 high-reimbursement generic drugs, and billed for medications that were medically unnecessary and often never given to anyone. No one was checking, so the money just flowed.

This man had six prior fraud convictions. He was out on bond, waiting to be sentenced in another fraud case, when he started this one. The system let a six-time fraudster bill it for $269 million because it turned off the one safeguard that would have caught him.

And he is a small piece of it. Investigators in the report estimate the country loses up to a trillion dollars a year to this kind of fraud, and that most of it ends up overseas with criminal networks, funding things far worse than mansions and baseball cards. Once the money leaves the country, they say, it is almost never recovered.

The lesson is the same one I come back to constantly. When nobody spending the money is spending their own, and nobody is guarding the door, the bill lands on you. Randall's mansion was paid for out of the same pot your taxes fund.

We built our pharmacy to be the opposite of a system with nobody home. No mystery billing, no bottomless account, no third party writing invoices for drugs that never existed. You see what a medication actually costs and you decide.

@JoinCrowdHealth  made a sketch imagining the founding fathers designing American healthcare on purpose, and it is funny because every insane detail in it is real.

Picture George Washington being briefed. We will build the finest healthcare system in the world. Will it be affordable? No. How will people pay? Through their employer. What if they lose their job? Then they lose their doctor too. Who decides what is covered? Nobody knows. If a doctor recommends a treatment, who approves it? A man in a call center who will place you on hold.

It keeps going, and it keeps being true. Can a family find out the price before they get care? No. Can the hospital tell them? The hospital does not know either. How much is a bandage, three dollars or three hundred? Based on what? No one knows. Is the price posted anywhere? Yes, in a file with tens of thousands of numbers that no human can actually use. That last one is not a joke. Hospitals really do satisfy price transparency by publishing giant machine-readable files that are almost impossible to read.

Then the medicine. A patient will not get his drugs from the doctor or the maker. He gets them from a third man who touches no medicine, sees no patient, and sets the price in secret. What is he called? A pharmacy benefit manager. What does he do? No one really knows. There are three of them, and they control almost the entire market.

And the ending lands because it is the most real part. After all the waiting and the paperwork, roughly one in five claims gets denied. Not before the care. After. You are already stitched up, already home, and then a letter arrives saying it was not medically necessary. Decided by someone who was not there, was not your doctor, and by many accounts spent less than a minute on the file. That 1-in-5 number is real, ACA marketplace plans denied about 19% of in-network claims in 2024.

None of it has a logical reason. That is how you know it is the actual system and not a parody.

The good part is the fix is not complicated. Take the middleman out and the prices come back down to something real. We know what our drugs cost, and we will just tell you.

A few years ago I had my whole family on a health insurance plan. Me, my wife, our daughter. We paid around $1,600 a month for it. The deductible was $17,000.

That year was not a quiet one. Our daughter broke her leg. My wife was pregnant, so she went to every prenatal visit, delivered the baby, and had all the postpartum care that follows. A broken leg and a full pregnancy and delivery in a single year.

We still did not hit the deductible.

So we paid $1,600 every month, all year, and then paid for the broken leg and the baby out of our own pockets on top of it, because insurance covered none of it. We handed that company close to $20,000 in premiums and got nothing back in a year with a broken bone and a newborn in it. That is when the math stopped making sense to me.

A lot of people are running this same calculation right now and landing in the same spot. You pay every month for a card that only starts helping after you have already spent a small fortune, and most years you never get there. You are insured and uninsured at the same time.

The good news is that a huge share of what people actually use is cheap once you take the insurance games out of it. Generic medications, which are about 90% of prescriptions, are genuinely inexpensive. You do not need to clear a $17,000 deductible to afford them. You just need to see the real price.

We fired the insurance companies, so nobody sits in the middle inflating what you pay. You look up the actual cost and decide for yourself.

Someone posted their hospital bill for a 30-minute seizure, and it is a masterpiece of nonsense. The total came to $8,449.85. Insurance paid about half.

Look at what is on it. Ninety dollars for a bag of saline, which is salt water. Lab tests they never asked for, including a drug test they did not consent to and did not need. $47.29 just to collect their blood. Over $1,000 for "hydration," which is the salt water again, wearing a fancier name. $523.39 for the anti-seizure medication. And my personal favorite, $23.01 for "professional fees," whatever that means.

None of these numbers are real. They are not what anything actually cost, and they are not meant to be. A hospital bill is written for the insurance company, not for the patient.
